output.title: Designing against eval drift starts with one stop rule
output.body:
If you are automating a recurring workflow, eval drift is the practical question of how you will know the system is no longer matching the work it was built to handle. In a small business, that often shows up in customer emails, invoices, or lead handling. The model may look fine on the sample used to build it, then real language, edge cases, or a process change start pulling it off course.

The bounded decision is simple: define the workflow, the measurable outcome, and the stop rule before you automate. For example, if an assistant is classifying inbox messages, decide what “correct enough” means and what level of manual review means the system needs a reset. Any threshold here is a control, not a promise. If you have not agreed it in advance, you are just hoping the model stays polite. Hope is not a control system.

For owner-operators, the line that matters is human approval. If the workflow touches money movement or any other high-risk decision, the machine should not decide on its own. That is a current scope discipline, not a theory exercise. Build for alerts, review, and a clear handoff back to you when confidence drops or patterns change; in a pilot, that alerting is a design intent, not a claim that it already exists.

One practical next step: write one sentence for the workflow, such as “If X changes, we pause automation and review Y.” Then add the question, “How will I know if this system stops working?” That turns eval drift from an abstract AI concern into an operational boundary you can actually run.
